The aim of this course is to give very good knowledge of signal processing, analysis and modeling for wireless communication systems. The course provides a theoretic foundation for further studies on wireless communication systems.

Knowledge and understanding
      For a passing grade the student must

Competences and skills
      For a passing grade the student must

Judgement and approach
      For a passing grade the student must

Stochastic processes, stationary and non-stationary, are introduced with the single-input single-output (SISO) communication system as a motivating example. In this context, autocorrelation, cross- correlation, power spectral density (PSD), Doppler power spectrum, and delay power spectrum are introduced. The concept of signal space is introduced together with the notion of equivalent complex baseband representation. Basic probability theory is revisited and connected to the communication systems by addressing optimal estimation (MMSE) and detection with MAP-receivers using matched filters. Commonly appearing probability distributions are briefly covered. Classic error bounds such as the union bound and the Chernoff bound are introduced. Channel capacity and the sampling theorem is introduced.

Complex matrices such as unitary matrices, circulant matrices, Hermitian matrices are introduced and an introduction to matrix decomposition techniques is provided. Classic signal processing algorithms such as the fast Fourier transform (FFT) are revisited from a matrix perspective. In the context of a multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) communication system, matrices such as channel matrices, stochastic matrices, covariance matrices, and Gram matrices are introduced. The capacity for such a MIMO-system under consideration is derived and asymptotic results for, e.g., Marchenko-Pastur distributed singular values are derived. Previous concepts for scalar signals, such as the PSD, are generalized for vector-valued signals.

Markov processes and state space models are furthermore introduced with the Viterbi algorithm for equalization or convolutional coding as an example. Soft-in soft-out detection is covered. Subsequently, graphs and graphical models in communication receivers are introduced together with the concepts: factor graphs, sum-product and min-sum algorithms for message passing in graphs, and factor graphs with states. Examples of use cases include: decoding, equalization and MIMO-detection. Furthermore, an introduction to iterative methods for joint decoding and detection is covered. This includes the concepts of coded modulation, turbo equalization, coded MIMO and EXIT chart analysis.

Grading scale: TH - (U, 3, 4, 5) - (Fail, Three, Four, Five)
Assessment:
Passed home assignments and a written exam (5 hours) with problems that cover the course content.

The examiner, in consultation with Disability Support Services, may deviate from the regular form of examination in order to provide a permanently disabled student with a form of examination equivalent to that of a student without a disability.

Code: 0126. Name: Examination. 

Credits: 5.0. Grading scale: TH - (U, 3, 4, 5).
        
          Assessment: Written exam.
        
        
          The module includes: The whole course.
        
        
        
Code: 0226. Name: Home Assignments. 

Credits: 2.5. Grading scale: UG - (U, G).
        
          Assessment: Passed home assignments.
        
        
          The module includes: Written reports.

Assumed prior knowledge: 
        FMAA01 Calculus in One Variable, EITF75 (or EITG10), Systems and Signals, FMAB20, Linear algebra or equivalent;  study experience equivalent to 2 years of studies at a technical university.
        
The number of participants is limited to: No
